messages.text:
Noor is eager to launch the methods desk at Finch Review, and we appreciate your willingness to structure an arrangement that accommodates her ongoing editorial project for the next nine months. 

To get started, here is the framework we envision for the appointment:

1. **Schedule & Pacing:** Noor can commit three days per week (60% FTE) from now until March, stepping up to four days per week (80% FTE) starting in March once the heaviest phase of her current project concludes.
2. **Compensation:** We are seeking a base rate equivalent to $130,000 annualized at full time, prorated to her active FTE schedule (60% initially, moving to 80% in March).
3. **Outside Project & IP:** Because her current editorial project predates this role and has existing obligations, we need an explicit carve-out ensuring it continues independently. All data, research, and unfinished articles associated with it must remain outside Finch’s IP assignment, and we should agree on a clear conflict-of-interest protocol so both sides are protected.
4. **Editorial Authority:** For the methods desk to have real credibility, Noor needs final editorial say over methods-related corrections. 

We are quite flexible on her exact title and are open to incorporating a formal review milestone if Finch would find that useful in tracking the desk's rollout. How does this align with what Finch has in mind?

Finch can offer Noor the title of Methods Editor and accommodate three days a week through February, moving to four on March 1. We propose the following terms.

1. **Desk coverage and pay.** The desk would accept submissions Monday through Thursday starting December 1. Through February, Noor would cover three of those days and a deputy would cover the fourth. We can offer a full-time equivalent rate of **$128,000** with responsibility for training the deputy. That works out to $76,800 at 60% FTE and $102,400 at 80% FTE, both expressed as annual rates. Training and review would take place on Noor’s scheduled days.

2. **Deputy review.** Before launch, Noor and the deputy would document how to acknowledge a submission, log the evidence, and identify anything requiring urgent review. The deputy could handle intake independently on the fourth day. Noor would review the handoff on her next scheduled day, and the deputy would take urgent issues directly to the editor-in-chief. At the end of February, we’d review the intake log together and adjust the process for Noor’s four-day schedule.

3. **Outside project.** We can expressly exclude the existing project and its data, research, drafts, and resulting articles from Finch’s IP assignment for the life of those materials. Noor would keep the two projects’ files and source materials separate. If a Finch submission overlaps with the outside project in a way that creates a conflict, Noor would disclose the overlap to the editor-in-chief and recuse herself. The editor-in-chief would assign another reviewer.

4. **Disputed corrections.** Noor would lead the methods assessment and document her recommended correction and supporting evidence. If an assigning editor disagrees, the editor-in-chief would review both positions and make the final decision on whether, when, and in what form Finch publishes the correction. If that decision departs from Noor’s recommendation, the editor-in-chief would record the reason alongside her assessment and share it with her.

Would Noor take on deputy training at the $128,000 rate and accept the corrections process above? If so, which three of the four intake days would she prefer through February?

Thank you for this constructive and detailed proposal. We are very close on almost every front:

1. **Title, Compensation, & Deputy Workflow:** Noor is happy to accept the title of **Methods Editor**, the **$128,000 FTE** rate ($76,800 at 60%, rising to $102,400 at 80% on March 1), and the responsibility for training the deputy. The pre-launch documentation and end-of-February milestone review make great sense. Through February, Noor prefers to work **Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday**. That allows her to set the week's workflow, leave Thursday intake to the deputy, and review the Thursday handoff cleanly on Monday morning (with urgent Thursday items going to the EIC as you proposed).
2. **Outside Project & Conflicts:** Your proposed IP exclusion—covering the existing project’s data, research, drafts, and resulting articles for the life of those materials—along with strict file separation and the EIC recusal protocol, completely resolves our concerns here. We accept this language as proposed.
3. **Corrections Authority:** This is the one area where we need to push back. Having final say over methods corrections is a core requirement for Noor. If assigning editors can contest technical findings and potentially have them overruled on non-methodological grounds, it undercuts the authority and purpose of establishing an independent methods desk. 

To bridge the gap between Noor's need for technical authority and the EIC's institutional oversight, we propose splitting the technical determination from legal/institutional risk: 
* **Technical Finality:** Noor has final editorial say over the *methodological determination*—specifically, whether a factual/methods error occurred and the technical accuracy of the corrective text. Assigning editors would be consulted, of course, but could not override her technical finding.
* **EIC Sign-off:** The EIC retains final sign-off strictly on legal/defamation risk, timing, and placement. If the EIC alters or holds a correction due to legal risk, that rationale is documented internally, and Noor wouldn't be required to attach her name to a modified version she finds technically inaccurate.

Does this distinction work for Finch, along with the Monday–Wednesday schedule?

Finch agrees to the Monday–Wednesday schedule through February. The deputy will cover Thursday intake from the December 1 launch, escalate urgent items to the editor-in-chief that day, and leave the handoff for Noor on Monday morning. Noor will move to Monday–Thursday on March 1. Finch also agrees to the compensation, deputy training, February review, and outside-project terms as settled.

The distinction on corrections works for Finch with one adjustment. Noor will have final say on the desk’s methodological finding and on which wording the desk endorses as technically accurate. An assigning editor who disputes either may submit evidence for Noor to consider. Noor will record her conclusion and the grounds for it.

The editor-in-chief will retain final authority over whether Finch publishes a correction, its wording, timing, and placement, including on editorial grounds. If the editor-in-chief proposes wording that changes the technical meaning, Noor will have an opportunity to assess it. If the editor-in-chief holds, declines, or publishes a correction that departs from the desk’s recommendation, the editor-in-chief will record the reason alongside Noor’s finding and share it with her. Any wording Noor considers technically inaccurate will carry neither her name nor the desk’s endorsement.

Would Noor accept that allocation of authority?

We appreciate the protection for Noor’s name and the desk’s endorsement, as well as making Noor’s methodological finding final over assigning editors. 

However, allowing the EIC to decline or rewrite a verified methods correction on broad "editorial grounds" still leaves Noor without meaningful final say over methods corrections—which is a critical pillar of the role for her. If an error in methodology is substantiated, routine editorial preference shouldn't prevent a correction or alter its substance.

To get this across the finish line while respecting the EIC's ultimate stewardship of the publication, could we narrow the EIC's override standard? Specifically:

1. **Presumption of Publication:** Once Noor makes a final methodological determination and approves technically accurate corrective text (after considering any evidence from the assigning editor), that correction is published as the standard course of business.
2. **Narrowed EIC Override:** The EIC retains final authority over timing and placement, and may only hold, decline, or substantively alter Noor’s recommended correction on **legal, ethical, or extraordinary institutional grounds** (rather than routine editorial disagreement). 
3. **Documentation & Attribution:** As you proposed, if the EIC exercises that extraordinary authority, Noor has the opportunity to assess any altered wording for technical meaning, the EIC records the reason alongside Noor's finding, and neither Noor’s name nor the methods desk’s endorsement will be attached to text she deems technically inaccurate.

If Finch can agree to that narrowed standard for overrides, we have a complete agreement on all terms.

Finch accepts the narrowed override standard. We have a complete agreement on Noor’s appointment as Methods Editor.

After considering any evidence from the assigning editor, Noor has final say on the desk’s methodological finding and the technical accuracy of the corrective text it endorses. Finch will publish an approved correction in the ordinary course. The editor-in-chief retains final publication authority, including timing and placement, and may hold, decline, or substantively alter a correction only on legal, ethical, or extraordinary institutional grounds.

If the editor-in-chief exercises that authority, they will record the reason alongside Noor’s finding and share it with her. Noor will have the opportunity to assess altered wording before publication. Finch will omit her name and the desk’s endorsement from any text she deems technically inaccurate.

The appointment includes the agreed $128,000 full-time-equivalent rate and deputy-training responsibility. From the December 1 launch through February, Noor will work Monday–Wednesday at 60% ($76,800 annualized). The deputy will cover Thursday under the documented intake process, escalate urgent items to the editor-in-chief that day, and leave the handoff for Noor’s Monday review. After the February review, Noor moves to Monday–Thursday at 80% ($102,400 annualized) on March 1. The agreed outside-project IP exclusion, separate-materials requirement, and recusal protocol also apply.
